Title: Wake - can there be alternative errata?

Messages.Author: prea...@utanet.at
Messages.Body:
Ok, I thought I'd like to post my musings on the matter, after following
the other thread.
To begin with, I'm not advocating a change of the current Wake errata at
the moment. :)

Let's start with the original un-errataed Wake. I never thought of it
unbalanced, but this is probably because I've never seen it abused.
However, when I read about the possibilities I was "shocked". :)
IMO the main problem was that you could put the Wakes in as "fillers":
find a killer combo, fill the rest of the deck with Wakes up to 60
cards, there you go. That was clearly a matter that had to be changed.

To a lesser degree you still can dump the Wakes: you can put down
exactly 7. This you can do on the last action of your predator, so you
don't have to face *any* disadvantage.
If you did it during any other player's turn, it would be plain stupid.

Now, what would change if we had errata that allows you to replace at
the end of the *current* turn? In a 4-player game you could dump 3*7=21
Wakes. Still Bad IMO.

There came some new ideas up:
* "do not replace until after combat <original card text> and when you
replace the card, show it to all players." I believe this wouldn't
violate any rules regarding showing cards to other players in
tournaments, btw.
This solution has a certain "coolness" to it, but doesn't do anything
against the cycling. Even if combined with "do not replace until the
beginning of the next turn" it is still abusable. ("Hey, look, he just
picked up 7 other Wakes.")
* burn either 1 pool or blood to replace the card. Here the question is:
when should it be replaced? If you keep the original card text (after
combat), and you pay one blood to replace the Wake, it's nothing else as
exactly the same card as FA (if you don't intend to block, that is). We
wouldn't want that. If it would be possible to replace at the end of
turn, or at the beginning at your own next turn, it would be clearly
inferior to FA, and obsolete.
What if you burned 1 pool to replace it? "Do not replace until the
beginning of your next turn. You may burn 1 pool to replace this card
immediatly." Hm. It *surely* would stop mad cycling. (Provided it isn't
a mass pool gain deck...) It would act just like the card is now with
the current errata, except that you'd have the option to replace it
sooner for the tradeoff of a very valuable resource. *But* it has an
additional sentence to it, whereas the current errata has just, well, 2
or 3 additional words or so.

Well, if I think now about it, I'm beginning to like the "1-pool option"
for Wake errata... :)
For me it seems to be a possible middleway. How much is a non-reduced
handsize worth to you? If it's not worth the 1 pool per slot, then just
don't replace it. :)

These are just some musings of mine, some ideas have been taken
selfishly from the other thread, but I think it shows the Wake-balance
issue from another angle. I hope you weren't bored by my long posting.

Carl

bleed defense. Thus, I will use Wake."

Yes--you have a valid complaint in that if you use Wake to block your Prey, you
have a smaller hand size for longer than if you only block your Predator. This
is true. Thus, if you are concerned about this added cost, and you are playing
a deck that intends on blocking stuff, you use Forced. Wake is useful in
situations where you are not concerned with the loss of hand size (like 'cause
your main intention is to bounce your predator), or where the loss of hand size
is potentially worth the trade off for the bonus defensive abilities.

Sorrow wrote:
>>But it's never this simple. There are plenty of other reasons that you

These reasons are in most situations much less likely to occur than blocking or
bouncing. What other reaction cards get used all that often? Obedience,
Delaying Tactics, Dread Gaze (maybe), possibly Telepathic Counter. Reaction
cards (that do not directly result in either blocking or bleed bounce) are a
sorely underutilized resource (because they simply aren't that useful). The
number of times you will need to play them in a given game is pretty limited,
and if you find yourself in a situation where you need one, in all likelyhood,
the blood cost of FA will be a reasonable price to pay.

>>But if you are using light intercept, something that has a decent enough
chance of being enough but not 100%, you aren't going to be using FA
but Wake instead.>>

If you only have light intercept, you are foolish to be trying to block anyone
that is likely to have extra stealth, Forced or no. If you have a deck that can
reliably provide +1 intercept (say, from a Sports Bike), you should only be
using that intercept to block minions who you know you can block. Otherwise,
you are just helping your opponents cycle cards. This being said, if you are
playing such a deck, Forced is the appropriate card to use--either you know you
can block so you do, or you don't even try.

>>To save blood. If you don't have FA. There are a variety of reasons you'd
want to use Wake. However, in doing so, the cost is way too much if you
do so against your prey.>>

If you want to save the blood, you use Wake and don't worry about the hand
loss. If you want to block, you use Forced.

>>Right, but it is never a clear cut case of block *or* bleed bounce.>>

It usually is in the decks that I build. I know what defenses I plan on. If I
am building a deck that plans on blocking, I use Forced. If Iam building a deck
with no intercept, but reaction cards (Deflect, Delaying Tactics), I use Wake.

>>There are a host of other reactions you can take. And because it isn't
*just*
block or bounce, why should it be that the cost is extra in those cases?>>

But you know when you are building your deck what options are available to you
in the deck, so you can plan accordingly, in terms of Forced or Wake.

>>Please get out of this mentality. All reactions do not revolve around
blocking or bouncing.>>

Nah. I like this mentality. You are correct that not *all* reactions revolve
around blocking or bouncing, but I would suport the notion that *most* of them
do. In my experience,the *vast* bulk of the reasons people play Wake/Forced is
to either block or bounce.

>>It is in using these other reactions that the cost of Wake is greatly
increased.>>

Yes, it is. If the cost is too excessive, use Forced--it is a simple choice.
Either pay the blood or lose hand size for a while. I still use Wake all the
time.

>>It's never worth the trade off. FA will always clearly be better because
of that.>>

This is clearly a point of disagreement that cannot be reconciled. Again, I
still use Wake in half of the decks I have that use reaction cards. Even one of
them that blocks (it uses light intercept and other reaction cards).

Hardly a straw man, but "\/\/hatever". I'm Derek. I play the game
lots. I talk lots, too. I'm not on the Rules Team. I'm not the
NetRep. I'm just me. Why should you trust me... because I'm right?
Every time we ask the NetRep why a card was changed, he has an answer.
That is definitely not "no reason".

The golden tenets are there for an EXTREMELY good reason, especially
the "No repeat actions" rule. This is definitely not "warping the
game", although i'm curious why you think the Golden Tenets do.

Card text on Wake specifies "This vampire can play reaction cards and
attempt to block as though untapped" - the key word here is "can".
Contrast with 2nd Tradition, which states "Also usable by a tapped
Prince or Justicar, even if intercept is not yet needed, to untap and
attempt to block with +2 intercept." The key word "can" or "may" is
missing, and strict interpretation of card text discovers the ruling
that 2nd Tradition users MUST attempt to block.

The errata to Wake may seem to make little sense to you, but there is
plenty of precedent for permitting cards to be played when they have
no useful effect - hand-strike cards in combat while the opponent is
at long range, for example, or adding Conditioning to a bleed after a
block is declared hoping to fish up a stealth card. If someone wishes
to waste cards by playing them to no effect, that should be fine -
it's invariably harmful to them in the long run, so they are hoping
for a short-term improvement at the cost of long-term viability. It
should just not be possible to waste cards to guaranteed good effect.
Hence, the more complex errata to Wake, because if you block one card
from being wasted because it "isn't right", you should block cards
from being played when they do no good - can't play Undead Strength if
your opponent is at long, etc. And that would be an ENORMOUS pile of
errata to no significant use.

>from being played when they do no good - can't play Undead Strength if

Given the game's fundamental dynamic - that cards are replaced
immediately - I'd have thought you'd need to be tough on playing cards
for no effect otherwise people will do this at every opportunity to
get to cards which are some use immediately. But Wake appears to be
special in this regard - I assume that the other cards are not so easy
to abuse in this way. If Wake is special then it deserves special
treatment.

The trouble with the current errata is that it goes beyond the printed
text in a non-intuitive way and that it punishes ordinary use of the
card too. If the problem is that the card can be too easily played to
no effect then that's the thing that need fixing. Just forbid it.

But I'm not even convinced that this is the real problem. As I
understand it, the problem is that collapsing the deck makes it easier
to play broken combos. I don't know what these combos are but why are
they not being addressed directly? And why can't players just load up
with lots of copies of the combo cards instead of lots of Wake? Are
they rares?

Note BTW that deck collapsing is a standard tactic in Doomtown and
folk typically use this to leave themselves with a killer shootout
hand. It usually takes a while though and the game might be lost in
the meantime. That's because you only fill your hand once a turn
rather than continuously. There is a card which let you refill your
hand within your turn like VTES. This broke the game - leading to
infinite loops on turn 2 or 3 - and has now been given errata. Our
former Jyhad player, Tom Kassel, recently used similar thinking to
break the wargame Paths of Glory and that had to be given errata too.
Examples of convergent evolution, I'm thinking. Given its mechanics,
I'm surprised that VTES doesn't have more trouble in this area - why
doesn't the same tactic work with other, easy-to-play cards?

Andrew

errata, or eventually you'll stumble on broken things on your own -

copy handy. Most of us know the basic things like the Golden Tenets,

everyday play.

>Given the game's fundamental dynamic - that cards are replaced

Players only normally do it out of desperation - when they need things
to work RIGHT THEN or face being ousted. But, using the Undead
Strength example, normally you only put a certain amount of strike
cards in a deck. If you begin wasting those cards carelessly, you'll
quickly discover that you have no more strike cards when you actually
CAN use them to effect. You may save yourself from ousting the first
time, but often you'll find that you've jammed up on master cards,
maneuvers, and Rush actions and your next combat will be "hand strike
for 1... don't have the Undead Strength in hand". It's a significant
risk to do that sort of thing.

Wake is special because its ability is useful in -every- deck, and the
only resource required to use it is a tapped vampire, something which
is normally plentiful. So you build a 60 card deck and toss in 20
Wakes - now you have a normal 60 card deck that taps out taking
actions, knowing that it will always be able to defend against its
predator if necessary, OR dump enough Wakes to get to the offensive
cards for its own turn. Peter's concern is a real issue - there are a
lot of +1 stealth actions to dump Wake on.

>The trouble with the current errata is that it goes beyond the printed
>text in a non-intuitive way and that it punishes ordinary use of the
>card too. If the problem is that the card can be too easily played to
>no effect then that's the thing that need fixing. Just forbid it.

Actually, it just gives Wake a cost, where previously it had none.
('replace at end of combat' is extremely minimal, especially if you
intend for there to be no combat by playing Deflection, etc.) I
suspect that Wake's original intent was to emphasize blocking instead
of reaction cards, but the designers misjudged the effect Deflection's
existence would have on the game - and THAT effect is only significant
because bleed decks are the strongest decks.

>But I'm not even convinced that this is the real problem. As I
>understand it, the problem is that collapsing the deck makes it easier
>to play broken combos. I don't know what these combos are but why are
>they not being addressed directly? And why can't players just load up
>with lots of copies of the combo cards instead of lots of Wake? Are
>they rares?

Not quite. The broken combos -do- get addressed directly - see Return
to Innocence, and Golconda/Soul Gem. Collapsing the deck makes it
easier to play *ANY* combo, and makes it much more likely that those
combos will actually show up. It doesn't mean the combos are broken
though. It ALSO means that you can tap out against your prey playing
the combos, and still be able to defend against your predator with
minimal to no cost (can always dump the Wakes to get more combos).

You could try to load up with lots of copies of the combo cards, but
decks that neglect their defense in this way tend to fall down and go
boom unless the combo is EXTREMELY powerful. You may have seen
discussion regarding "Weenie Dominate Tap & Bleed", which basically
relies on a whole bunch of small vampires with Dominate and a deckful
of Misdirections, bleed cards, bleed modifiers, Deflection, and
Delaying Tactics. It carries no Wakes, errata'd or not, because it
moves extremely fast and doesn't NEED much defense. Its defense is
gaining pool by ousting people. It's feared far and wide, although
combat decks tend to make it go "pop!" and people tend to gang up on
it to make it go away.

The problem with it is, how do you errata weenie dominate? The most
key card in the deck is Misdirection, but to play it you spend one
pool per vampire you tap - it's a strong card, but I'm not certain
that it's overpowered especially EXCEPT in combination with weenie
hordes.

>Examples of convergent evolution, I'm thinking. Given its mechanics,
>I'm surprised that VTES doesn't have more trouble in this area - why
>doesn't the same tactic work with other, easy-to-play cards?

Most of the easy-to-play cards are combat cards. Most combat decks

they not being addressed directly? And why can't players just load up

they rares?>>

The problem with unerrataed Wake is that it has a completely insufficient cost
for its effect. Jyhad is a game with a very strict cost/effect paradigm, and
Wake completely circumvented this paradigm. All cards have a cost--the more
powerful card, the more expensive the cost. Some costs are requiring
disciplines (discipline cards), costing blood (more powerful discipline cards),
or conditionality (cards like Fake Out or Dead End Alley). Wake had a cost (do
not redraw until after combat) that was found to be completey insufficient for
the power of the card, and consequently, became the *only* card in the game
that could be played for no effect and cycled for free. Thus, it needed to be
errataed to be brought into line with other cards and the cost/effect paradigm.

You may or may not be aware of the Sabbat version--Forced Awakening. It is
essentially similar to Wake, but you get to re-draw it immediately, but if you
fail to sucessfully block, the reacting vampire burns a blood. When compared to
the pre-errata Wake, FA was simply not as good. FA, however, was an example of
how Wake *should* have been designed. To have both FA and unerrataed Wake in
the game environment was a bad thing, thus Wake was weakened to what it is now.

*Because* Fake Out/Dodge are played during combat, they automatically
take up the problem of "Do not replace...." because of the fact that
they are played during combat. Similarly, because "Do not replace...."
means "Do not replace until after combat, or until this action
concludes" an action card like Arson has the built in disadvantage that
you won't replace it (and, say, draw a stealth card).

Wake, being a reaction card, doesn't do any of that. Being a reaction
card, you're never going to *have* to do anything - unless you put a
cumbersome and unwieldy errata upon it ("You must react or block, or
play sufficient intercept to meet the current action's stealth,
or...."). As a result, Wake can just be cycled immediately. The cost
on Fake Out really is a cost - because you are in combat. The cost on

among the less common card games, so far as I can tell, in having the
constant replace mechanism, in that when you play a card, you (normally)
replace it very quickly. Most other games tend to have the "Draw a
card" phase somewhere near the start of your turn.

As such, in V:TES, terms like "card advantage" never really come into
their own, as they do in Magic. Drawing more cards than your opponent
isn't *quite* such a guarantee of doing well, because you aren't getting
an advantage over the basic rules. In Magic, everyone draws one card a
turn. In V:TES, everyone could, theoretically, draw their entire deck
in one turn, just by playing enough cards - continually pressing,
maneuvering, preventing, stealthing etc.

*depending on your deck* it might be. But then, we have three very
similar cards in Protean - Wolf Claws, Claws of the Dead, Bone Spur.
Each has a different advantage. Myself, I simply adore Claws of the
Dead. The maneuver at superior is, IMO, worth its weight in gold, and a

Note: I was not privy to any such discussions either. All that follows
is conjecture, combined with bits and pieces that seem to have come up
from debates with LSJ etc.

1) There seems to be a clear desire to - except where *absolutely*
necessary - keep errata short.

2) Any errata which goes along the lines of "When you play Wake, you
must also play sufficient intercept to be able to block (either from
permanent sources or from transient sources), or play another reaction
card" is more difficult to explain to new players. A new player can
look at the card as it stands and, were they to turn up to a tournament,
would only be slightly impinged by Wake - it gets replaced a bit later.
If they suddenly found that they had to play other cards with it, all
their preparation along the lines of "Well, if it becomes a bit of a
drag in my deck, I'll just react with it and ditch it" becomes
meaningless. They can still do that with the current errata - it's just
slowed down.

3) Ditto point 2) regarding changing it to a burn blood penalty/cost.
The current errata is merely an annoyance to player working around the
text, and a mild spanner in the works. But if they can't afford the
blood, because their deck never planned for it, you've just screwed them
over. Only a couple of the errata *really* change a card (Fame being
the 'worst' offender (but then Fame was a hideous card to start with),
Mind Rape being slightly less bad). Keeping those to an absolute
minimum is best. Strengthening the delay penalty is a mild change.
Adding/Changing a blood cost penalty is a more major change, as would
adding a "Show the card to...." change be.

Excellent strategy. The primary purpose of the game is to provide a fun
way for a group of friends (or enemies :-) to pass the time.

When teaching the game, ignoring the errata is a valid option - it decreases
the learning curve. As players get more experience, however, it might be
beneficial to look at the clarifications and rulings to double-check one's
playing style. And even if one doesn't use the errata, it would probably
still be a good idea to look over the errata to see what typos have been
corrected (the Malkavian requirement on Malkavian Dementia, for example)
as well as what "problems" have been perceived in other groups.

If your group begins to encounter some of these same problems, you
may find that the game ceases to be fun any more. At that stage, you
have a few options:

1) stop playing.
2) continue playing, but with a "gentleman's agreement" not to play in
an "un fun" way.
3) adopt some or all of the errata, as you need it to maintain the fun level
of the game
4) adopt some of your own house rules as opposed to the errata to
address the problems in way that you find to be superior to the official
rules.

Of course, if you end up playing in any tournaments or other setting where
players from other groups besides your own are involved, the default
method of play includes all of the official errata (probably some circular
definition in there, but you get the idea).

> text in a non-intuitive way and that it punishes ordinary use of the
> card too. If the problem is that the card can be too easily played to
> no effect then that's the thing that need fixing. Just forbid it.

Difficult in practice. But see 4) above.

Good luck to youi and your group, and welcome aboard!
